findings.title: Cross-Chain TxDataHiding Crypto Heist: A Very Chainful Process (Part 1)
findings.summary_md: Ransom-ISAC's original disclosure of the DPRK-attributed XCTDH campaign, investigated from a malicious private GitHub repository impersonating node-react-e-commerce with the payload hidden in tailwind.config.js (SHA256 16df15306f966ae5c5184901747a32087483c03eebd7bf19dbfc38e2c4d23ff8). It documents TRON wallets TMfKQEd7TJJa5xNZJZ2Lep838vrzrs7mAP and TXfxHUet9pJVU1BgVkBAbrES4YUc1nGzcG acting as indexes into BSC transaction calldata carrying XOR-encrypted JavaScript, delivered via fake LinkedIn job offers, with C2 at 23[.]27[.]20[.]143:27017. The BSC sender wallet 0x9BC1355344B54DEDf3E44296916eD15653844509 identified here was still in use in the September 2026 samples, confirming the same operator roughly a year on.

findings.title: NullReceiver's Blank Crypto Transfers Solves the Challenges of EtherHiding
findings.summary_md: OpenSourceMalware (Paul McCarty) published the first public description of the recipient-address C2 encoding, named NullReceiver, found via static analysis of two trojanised npm packages, bianira-ui@1.27.0 and fluid-type-ui@2.0.8, attributed to the DPRK Contagious Interview campaign. A zero-value, zero-data Ethereum transfer from attacker wallet 0xa322e5f3d311d3080e6f0121063e9adc2490ef1a carries the C2 endpoint 166.88.134.62 encoded in the recipient address bytes, with no smart contract and no calldata to fingerprint. Ransom-ISAC explicitly credits this post for the technique and the name in its September HashHiding report.

findings.title: XCTDH Adopts Hash Hiding
findings.summary_md: The primary research behind this story, by Ellis Stannard and Nick Smart, published three days before the first news rewrites. It documents the _Z module, 69,470 characters of base-91 and control-flow-flattened JavaScript delivered in the C2 /init response, which scans Ethereum mainnet via public RPC providers (publicnode.com, drpc.org, blastapi.io) for transfers from signal wallet 0x33ff3edaf55a8e03dcbc7cb40d498a49cd499891 and decodes the C2 endpoint from the first six bytes of the recipient address. Ninety days of on-chain collection show 2,655 beacon transactions from 23 June 2026 to 21 September 2026 with four C2 rotations, currently 181[.]214[.]149[.]148:443, plus a YARA rule and full IOC tables.
